blocks.body: # TRECVID 2026 Video QA: Field Guide and Submission Plan

## Executive Summary

TRECVID is the video-evaluation program within the Text REtrieval Conference (TREC), run by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).

- **The job has two outputs.** Answer Generation (AG) requires exactly ten ranked natural-language answers plus per-answer time for every video question; Multiple Choice (MC) requires a full ranking of the four supplied options. Both now use JSON.
- **The 2026 test is broader and harder.** NIST plans 1,457 held-out YouTube Shorts, roughly 400 licensed movie scenes, new Shorts, and auto-generated QA. Some clips may reach six minutes, and the known holdout is 54.5% causal despite the original 500-video training set having no causal examples.
- **The 2025 leaders were metric-specific.** CERTH-ITI posted the highest current AG content scores (METEOR 0.2604, STS 0.3510; a near-duplicate CERTH run had BERTScore 0.9034). NII_UIT posted the highest current MC scores (Top-1 0.7810, MRR 0.8671). There was no official composite AG winner.
- **Recommended posture: enter both and build one shared evidence pipeline.** Decode each video reliably, sample useful frames, convert speech to text, and gather local visual detail once; then use thin AG and MC output heads. Treat MC as the more predictable score target. Start with NII-style dense frames and tiles, test CERTH-style multi-view aggregation, and defer a learned reranker until direct AG answers are strong. Verify registration and the movie agreement now, then freeze a working baseline before the July 17 AG release.

## Contents and reading paths

This guide is intentionally deep. The chapter numbers below repeat in the large headings throughout the report.

**10-minute orientation:** Executive Summary → Chapter 3 → Chapter 7 → Chapter 8.

**Understand the field from scratch:** Chapters 1 → 2 → 3 → 4.

**Plan and build a 2026 system:** Chapters 1 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 8.

1. **Task, rules, and outputs** — what the competition asks for and how it is scored.
2. **Models and scoring in plain English** — how video, audio, and language components fit together.
3. **2025 submissions and leaders** — all published runs, strongest results, and scoring traps.
4. **Team architectures and public repositories** — how the seven teams assembled their systems.
5. **Fine-tuning and public weights** — LoRA/QLoRA, data, compute, available checkpoints, and a safe training plan.
6. **Literature and transferable ideas** — six research mechanisms and their competition-ready experiments.
7. **Recommended 2026 system** — one evidence engine, separate AG/MC heads, and strict validation.
8. **Run plan, calendar, and immediate actions** — which submissions to build and what to do next.
9. **Questions, caveats, and glossary** — unresolved organizer questions and newcomer definitions.

> **Navigation tip:** on a phone, scan for “Chapter” in the large headings. On a computer, use Find (Ctrl/Cmd+F) with a chapter number or the bold title above.

## Chapter 1 · Start here: this is a benchmark, not a conventional training contest

NIST releases videos and questions, teams run fully automatic systems, and NIST's Evalbase web portal validates submitted rankings. Hidden reference answers are then used for uniform scoring. In **AG**, the answer itself is open text, so both correctness and wording matter; in **MC**, the correct text is already among four options, so the problem is ranking.

The seven published question categories are temporal, causal, audio/multimodal, multi-hop, people-object interaction, counting, and commonsense. A `Video_ID` may be a YouTube identifier or a local movie filename, so the ingestion layer must handle both. Read the [official 2026 task page](https://www-nlpir.nist.gov/projects/tv2026/vqa.html) before treating any example schema as final.

## Chapter 2 · A submission is a pipeline, not just a model name

A **model architecture** is a blueprint, a **checkpoint** is one trained set of weights, and a **submission pipeline** adds media decoding, frame selection, audio handling, prompting, ensembling, normalization, ranking, and JSON validation. Two teams can use the same model family and obtain very different results because the surrounding pipeline controls what evidence the model ever sees.

**How to read the image below:** the sampler chooses pages from a flipbook, the vision encoder turns patches into numeric “visual words,” the connector translates those words for the language model, and the final head converts raw output into the exact competition contract. A failure in any box can dominate the choice of backbone.

## The model families differ mainly in how they turn media into language tokens

[Qwen2.5-Omni](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20215) has native, time-aligned audio and video encoders. [Qwen2.5-VL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13923), [InternVL3.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18265), and [Aria](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05993) are principally visual-and-text systems, so teams supplied speech through Whisper transcripts. [VideoLLaMA2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07476) explicitly mixes spatial and temporal features and has an audio-video variant; [VideoLLaMA3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.13106) focuses on efficient visual tokenization and frame pruning. Gemini Flash is proprietary, so its team-specific internals should remain a black box.

**The practical comparison is not ‘which name is newest?’** It is whether the selected checkpoint supports the required evidence, fits the frame/tile budget, and exposes a reliable way to generate ten AG candidates or directly rank four MC options. The table is an architecture guide, not a cross-paper leaderboard.

## The known 2026 holdout is an out-of-distribution causal test

**Causal questions account for 794 of the 1,457 held-out Shorts, or 54.5%.** The original 500-video training split contained no causal examples. This makes question routing, external public training data, robust zero-shot reasoning, and category-level validation more important than simply fitting the small official training set.

The chart covers only the held-out Shorts. NIST has not published exact category counts for the movie, new-Shorts, or auto-generated-QA additions, so those are intentionally omitted.

## Scoring separates answer quality from answer order

AG uses three content-similarity families—METEOR, BERTScore, and Semantic Textual Similarity (STS)—plus Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) for ordering. The 2026 page says results will be reported at top 1, 5, and 10, but the exact aggregation code is not yet published. MC uses Top-1 accuracy and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR).

Treat the [public scorer](https://github.com/gawad-nist/VQA) as a 2025 regression tool only: its README says it still needs a 2026 JSON and cutoff update. Pin the final organizer commit when announced, and retain raw per-query answers so every run can be rescored.

## Chapter 3 · The 2025 pilot drew seven teams and 29 official runs

The first VQA pilot received **20 AG runs from seven teams** and **nine MC runs from five teams**. The complete overview inventory is below. The current score appendices are narrower: 12 AG rows and seven MC rows. TJUMI supplied corrected files after official results; those corrections are not mixed into the official inventory or leaderboards here.

## CERTH led open-ended answer similarity, but AG had no single overall winner

**CERTH run 2 has the highest published METEOR (0.2604) and STS (0.3510); CERTH run 4 has the highest BERTScore (0.9034).** The 0.0001 BERTScore difference from CERTH run 1 is not practically meaningful and has no published significance test.

WHU shows 1.0000 NDCG, but those systems returned one answer per query and the 2025 scorer hard-codes a one-item list to NDCG 1.0. That value therefore does not demonstrate superior ten-answer ranking. Use the chart for shape and the table for exact lookup.

## The 2026 ten-answer rule turns tail quality into the central AG problem

The [2025 scorer](https://github.com/gawad-nist/VQA) averaged content similarity across every returned answer. CERTH's single-answer run therefore led METEOR and STS, while [CERTH's post-hoc top-1 analysis](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/papers/CERTH-ITI.avs.vqa.pdf) showed the main ten-view system had the stronger first answer. The [NII per-response file](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/appendices/trec2025-vqa-gen/Aria8x3.5B_VidLLaMa.per_response.csv) tells the same story: rank-1 METEOR was about **0.212** versus **0.173** across all ten answers, and rank-1 STS was about **0.310** versus **0.270** overall.

In 2026, fewer than ten answers will be rejected. The practical response is not ten loose paraphrases: generate a larger pool, normalize and cluster it, remove weak or redundant candidates, and train or calibrate a ranker so ranks 6–10 do not erase the quality of rank 1.

## NII_UIT led Multiple Choice, with CERTH close behind

**NII_UIT's `HIGHEST_PIPELINE` has the highest current appendix values: 0.7810 Top-1 and 0.8671 MRR.** CERTH run 2 follows at 0.7679 and 0.8629—a 1.31 percentage-point Top-1 gap and a 0.0042 MRR gap.

These current appendix values average 1,982 evaluated records. Workshop papers used all 2,000 ground-truth rows in the denominator while 18 unavailable videos contributed nothing, producing slightly lower decimals (0.774/0.859 for NII). The ordering is unchanged; this report uses the current appendix by default.

## Chapter 4 · Three design patterns mattered more than any single model family

**First, present better evidence.** [NII_UIT](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/papers/NII_UIT.vqa.pdf) used uniform temporal coverage, spatial tiles for small details, Whisper transcripts, question-aware prompts, and concise normalization. **Second, aggregate multiple views.** [CERTH-ITI](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/papers/CERTH-ITI.avs.vqa.pdf) fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and pooled predictions from ten random frame subsets; direct option-letter logit pooling worked far better than confidence scoring full answer strings. **Third, separate generation from ranking.** [HLTCOE](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/papers/HLTCOE.vqa.pdf) generated multiple Qwen2.5-VL candidates and experimented with a listwise pointer reranker. The [WHU-NERCMS](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/papers/WHU-NERCMS.avs.vqa.pdf) and [kslab](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/papers/kslab.vqa.pdf) papers cover the remaining published team methods.

The repeated lesson is architectural: video decoding, temporal coverage, audio/text evidence, and ranking discipline can move results without requiring the largest possible model. The table below places every team in that design space.

## The teams were separated more by evidence and ranking choices than by model size

The matrix shows whether eight architecture components were **explicitly documented** for each team. A dark cell (`1`) means reported; a light cell (`0`) means the reviewed public material did not document it. Zero must not be read as proof that the underlying model lacked the capability—especially for Gemini and the sparsely documented TJUMI pipeline.

**Read across a row to see the system strategy.** CERTH combines native audio, task tuning, multiple visual views, and direct MC scoring. NII keeps weights frozen but adds transcripts and spatial tiles. HLT separates candidate generation from a learned reranker. WHU and kslab use generated-answer embeddings for MC. This is a component map, not a quality score.

## Four architecture patterns explain all seven teams

The images below group the published systems by **how they gather evidence and turn it into a ranked answer**. They are architecture maps, not performance rankings. Where tcna or TJUMI did not publish an intermediate stage, the diagram labels that gap instead of guessing.

## The two linked repositories are idea libraries, not frozen submissions

NIST links the [NII_UIT framework](https://github.com/aiclub-uit/TrecVID2025_VQA) and the [HLTCOE reranker](https://github.com/adoptedirelia/TREC2025-HLTCOE) as starters. Both repositories were created after the evaluation, have no tagged submission release, and omit critical run-time pieces.

NII contains useful codec handling, frame extraction, tiling, speech transcription, and multi-backend inference, but the exact winning configuration is absent and paper features such as question routing are not implemented. HLTCOE's research objective is valuable, but its checked public code has missing imports, a dataset-builder error, a training/inference format mismatch, and no released Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters. Reimplement the ideas in a tested, licensed pipeline.

## Chapter 5 · Fine-tuning can help—but it is not the first repair

**Beginner answer:** fine-tuning means continuing training from an existing checkpoint so its behavior shifts toward this task. It is useful when a repeatable error remains **after** the system reliably decodes the video, retrieves the right moments, includes speech or sound when needed, and emits valid AG/MC output.

For this competition, the safest order is **frozen baseline → learned ranker or LoRA/QLoRA adapter → larger adapter experiment → full fine-tune only as a last resort**. A missing causal moment, broken video, omitted alarm sound, or leaked split will not become correct because more weights were updated.

**Recommended first train:** a QLoRA adapter on a 2–4B instruction checkpoint plus a separate evidence-aware AG ranker. Keep the vision/audio encoders frozen initially. Compare against the exact same frozen baseline and evidence pack before escalating to 7–9B.

## What “fine-tuning” actually means

- **Checkpoint:** a saved set of model weights. “Base” or “pretrained” checkpoints know broad patterns but are not necessarily trained to follow questions; **Instruct** or **post-trained** checkpoints are the normal competition starting point.
- **SFT — supervised fine-tuning:** show the model an input and the answer or behavior it should produce. SFT is the *learning objective*; it does not say how many weights change.
- **LoRA:** freeze the checkpoint and train small low-rank adapter matrices. The saved adapter is much smaller than another full copy of the model.
- **QLoRA:** LoRA while the frozen checkpoint is loaded in 4-bit form. It reduces base-weight memory, but video activations and context still cost memory.
- **Ranker/head tuning:** train only the final judge that orders AG candidates or scores MC options. The video generator can remain frozen.
- **Preference training — DPO, MPO, or RL variants:** teach that one output is better than another. This can improve judging or reasoning, but it adds data and evaluation complexity.
- **Full fine-tune:** update the whole model. It uses much more memory and risks forgetting general skills; it is rarely the right first move on a 500-video domain set.

Official [TRL SFTTrainer guidance](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/v0.26.0/en/sft_trainer) supports vision-language training, and [PEFT LoRA](https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/main/en/package_reference/lora) / [quantization guidance](https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/developer_guides/quantization) covers adapter and QLoRA setup. For VLMs, preserve image/video tokens—TRL explicitly warns against text-style truncation that can remove them.

## What last year’s teams actually fine-tuned

The word covered **three different system choices**.

**CERTH-ITI adapted the multimodal model.** Its [official 2025 paper](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/papers/CERTH-ITI.avs.vqa.pdf) reports LoRA SFT of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B on the organizer’s 500 training videos: 10 frames / 1,024 visual tokens, five epochs, rank 16, alpha 64, on one 24 GB RTX 4090. Its participant-reported MC ablation moved Top-1 from 73.2% frozen to 74.4% fine-tuned; adding ten-view aggregation reached 76.1%. That is evidence of a modest adapter gain and a larger combined system gain—not proof that tuning alone caused the final leaderboard position.

**HLTCOE adapted the judge, not the video generator.** Its [participant paper](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/papers/HLTCOE.vqa.pdf) describes LoRA on a listwise reranker using 500 examples, a 90/10 split, five epochs, rank 16, alpha 32, and dropout 0.05. The private submission adapter was not released.

**NII_UIT kept both main backbones frozen.** Its [paper](https://trec.nist.gov/pubs/trec34/papers/NII_UIT.vqa.pdf) instead invested in timestamped speech, time-spaced frames, local tiles, and question-type prompts. That is an important baseline: sometimes the best “adaptation” is better evidence.

## What data a defensible fine-tune needs

One training example should retain **video identity, question, exact visual/audio evidence or timestamps, answer target, output format, and provenance**. For MC, store all four original option strings and the correct option. For AG ranking, store the candidate pool, evidence references, relevance/order labels, and how those labels were created.

The critical rule is **split by video and source before training**, not by QA row. If two questions from the same clip land in train and validation, the model can memorize scenes, people, subtitles, or audio and look more general than it is. Near-duplicate clips, movie segments, channel families, and source collections also stay together.

Use 100–500 checked examples to prove the pipeline; roughly 1,000–5,000 diverse grounded examples is a reasonable first adapter band; 10,000+ can support broader adaptation. These are planning heuristics, not magic thresholds. A small, balanced, timestamped set is often more informative than a large pile of unverified generated answers.

## What compute, storage, and software are needed

**GPU memory:** a 2–4B QLoRA experiment is the comfortable one-workstation starting point. A bounded 7–9B adapter run can fit one 24 GB GPU—the CERTH recipe is a real example—but 48–80 GB gives safer room for more frames, higher resolution, and useful batch sizes. Full fine-tuning usually means multiple GPUs.

**Disk and data operations:** keep the original media manifest, normalized videos, frame/audio caches, training JSONL or Parquet, exact split files, base revision, adapter checkpoints, optimizer state for resumable runs, metrics, prompts, and environment lockfile. Media caches can easily require tens to hundreds of gigabytes even when the adapter itself is only hundreds of megabytes.

**Software stack:** use the model’s official processor plus pinned versions of Transformers, TRL, PEFT, bitsandbytes for QLoRA, and Accelerate/FSDP or DeepSpeed only when distribution is required. The official [Qwen3-VL repository includes fine-tuning code](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-VL/tree/main/qwen-vl-finetune). Run a 10-example overfit test and checkpoint-reload test before spending on a long run.

The ranges below are planning bands—not guarantees. Video tokens, resolution, clip length, precision, attention kernels, gradient checkpointing, batch size, and whether the vision/audio towers are frozen can move any recipe to the next tier.

## Public weights: a practical 2026 shortlist

**Default path:** start with [Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct), run [InternVL3.5-4B](https://huggingface.co/OpenGVLab/InternVL3_5-4B) as an architecture-diverse comparison, and use [SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM2-2.2B-Instruct) as the cheap dataset/training sandbox. Escalate to 8B only if a controlled learning curve supports it.

For sound-heavy questions, visual-only models need timestamped ASR plus a non-speech audio path. A frozen native-audio expert such as [Qwen2.5-Omni-7B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Omni-7B) or [MiniCPM-o-4.5](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/MiniCPM-o-4_5) can handle speech and sound, but omni-model fine-tuning is substantially more complex.

“Public weights” is not one promise. Check whether access is immediate or gated; whether the license covers your use; whether custom code is required; whether the model card names its training data; and whether the checkpoint is **base, Instruct, Thinking, SFT-only, preference-optimized, or task-specialized**. Pin the exact Hub revision and processor.

## Public fine-tuned models: use them as specialists, not magic replacements

There are useful originator-released video fine-tunes: [VideoChat-R1.5](https://huggingface.co/OpenGVLab/VideoChat-R1_5-7B) revisits predicted evidence intervals; [Video-R1](https://huggingface.co/Video-R1/Video-R1-7B) exposes public video SFT/RL weights; [SAGE-MM Molmo2](https://huggingface.co/allenai/SAGE-MM-Molmo2-8B-SFT_RL) learns when to call ASR and temporal/high-resolution tools; and [VideoRefer-VideoLLaMA3](https://huggingface.co/DAMO-NLP-SG/VideoRefer-VideoLLaMA3-7B) specializes in spatial-temporal grounding.

Their training objectives often produce long reasoning traces, tool-call JSON, multiple-choice answers, or boxes—not TRECVID’s exact final AG/MC contract. The safest use is as a **retriever, verifier, judge, or grounding specialist** behind a thin competition output head.

Do not treat a Hub “finetunes” count as evidence of quality. Adopt a derivative only if it documents the exact base revision, license, training data, objective, evaluation setup, processor, and reproducible code. The CERTH and HLTCOE competition-specific 2025 adapters themselves were not released as reproducible public checkpoints.

## A safe fine-tuning plan for this year

1. **Freeze the evaluation contract.** Build video/source-exclusive train, validation, and locked test manifests. Define AG top-1/top-5/top-10, MC Top-1/MRR, option-order stability, evidence recall, latency, and schema validity.
2. **Run frozen checkpoints on identical evidence.** Compare SmolVLM2-2.2B, Qwen3-VL-4B, and InternVL3.5-4B. Add one frozen native-audio expert only for questions where sound is diagnostic.
3. **Label the failure, not just the answer.** Mark decode, retrieval, OCR, ASR/audio, temporal ordering, reasoning, candidate generation, ranking, and format failures. Fine-tune only the stage with repeatable residual error.
4. **Train two small experiments first.** (a) a QLoRA SFT adapter on the 2–4B primary model; (b) a separate evidence-aware listwise AG ranker or MC option scorer. Keep the vision/audio encoders frozen.
5. **Use learning curves and ablations.** Train on 25%, 50%, and 100% of the clean set; repeat at least two seeds; compare the same evidence pack; report per-category effects and confidence intervals. Keep an oracle-evidence run to tell retrieval from reasoning.
6. **Escalate only on a validation gate.** Move to a 7–9B adapter when the small-model pipeline is correct and the gain is capacity-limited. Add an ensemble only when errors are complementary. Full fine-tuning is a no-go unless adapters plateau on thousands of diverse examples and the expected gain justifies multi-GPU operations.
7. **Package reproducibility with every run.** Save base revision, adapter, processor, prompts, evidence IDs/timestamps, split hash, environment, seed, training curve, evaluation outputs, and schema-validation receipt.

**Recommended submission portfolio:** frozen evidence-first baseline; 4B QLoRA adapter; ranker-only variant; architecture-diverse frozen or tuned comparison; and an audio-specialist ensemble only if the audio subset gains without harming silent questions.

## What fine-tuning cannot repair

- **The relevant moment was never sampled.** Fix retrieval and frame coverage.
- **Speech or a non-speech cue was discarded.** Add timestamped ASR and an audio branch.
- **The label is wrong, ambiguous, or generated from the test answer.** Audit or remove it.
- **The same video or near-duplicate appears in train and validation.** Re-split before trusting any gain.
- **MC option order is a shortcut.** Permute options and test no-video controls.
- **AG candidates are repetitive or unsupported.** Improve generation, deduplication, evidence scoring, and listwise ranking.
- **The output violates exact IDs, ranks, counts, option strings, timing, or JSON.** Use a deterministic schema validator after the model.
- **A public checkpoint has unclear license or lineage.** Do not build the submission around it until those terms are resolved.

A fine-tune is successful only when it beats the frozen baseline on a locked, source-separated validation set **and** preserves evidence quality, calibration, runtime, and schema reliability.

## Chapter 6 · Competition-adjacent research points to one system pattern

This is not one new model architecture. It is a way to divide the job into **six testable problems**: choose what the model sees, check whether it found the right moments, preserve both the timeline and small details, keep speech and other sound, connect evidence into a grounded explanation, and select the final answer without being fooled by wording or option order.

### A running example for the whole chapter

Imagine a 40-second kitchen video. At 8 seconds a pan begins to smoke, at 15 seconds an alarm sounds, and at 27 seconds a person opens a window. The question is: **“Why did the person open the window?”** A credible system must find separated moments, connect them in the right order, and resist easy but unsupported guesses such as “to cool the room.”

### Five terms translated before we use them

- **Visual token:** a unit of model input created from image patches. It is not cryptocurrency. More frames and larger crops consume more of the context and compute budget.
- **Retrieval:** finding the moments that contain useful evidence.
- **Fusion:** combining facts from more than one retrieved moment.
- **Grounding:** keeping a timestamp, frame, crop, transcript span, or sound event that supports a claim.
- **Calibration:** making a score behave like reliability rather than reflecting answer length, repeated wording, or MC option position.

The short version is: **find the evidence, preserve it, combine it, then decide.** The next six sections reuse the kitchen example in prose, add a different concrete example in each image, identify the closest papers and 2025 teams, and end with one controlled TRECVID experiment.

## Idea 1 — Spend the frame budget on coverage and relevance

**Plain meaning:** a video-language model usually does not watch every video frame at full resolution. A sampler chooses a small set of frames, and the vision encoder turns each frame into many visual tokens. A longer or higher-resolution input therefore costs more memory, context, latency, and often money. The real question is not “How many frames can we send?” but “Which combination is least likely to omit the answer?”

**Everyday analogy:** imagine receiving a 200-page security-camera printout but being allowed to keep only 12 pages. Uniform sampling is like keeping every seventeenth page. Question-only selection is like searching for pages that resemble the word “window.” A safer hybrid reserves some pages for the whole story and spends the rest on likely evidence.

**Kitchen example:** a uniform sampler might capture the person opening the window but miss the earlier smoke. A question-relevance sampler might over-focus on frames containing the window and also miss the cause. A coverage-plus-query sampler keeps beginning, middle, and end coverage, then adds smoke-, alarm-, and window-related moments.

**What the literature adds:** [KFS-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14017) makes multi-scene coverage measurable; [BOLT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21483) samples from a question-relevance distribution instead of taking only the top-scoring frames; [VideoTree](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19209) searches a coarse-to-fine temporal hierarchy.

**Closest 2025 systems:** NII_UIT's roughly twelve time-spaced frames emphasize coverage. CERTH-ITI's multiple random views increase the chance that at least one view contains the evidence. Neither comparison proves causality; they provide sensible baselines for a controlled selector test.

**TRECVID test:** at fixed budgets of 12, 24, and 32 frames, compare uniform-only, question-only, random multi-view, and half-uniform plus half-question selection. Record selected timestamps, total tokens, latency, answer score, and—on a small labeled slice—required-evidence recall.

## Idea 2 — Finding evidence and combining evidence are different skills

**Retrieval** asks whether the system found the right moments. **Fusion** asks whether the model combined those moments correctly. Treating them as one end-to-end score hides the cause of failure and encourages expensive model changes when the sampler may be the real problem.

**Everyday analogy:** retrieval is the detective collecting the correct photographs; fusion is the jury using those photographs to reach the right conclusion. A perfect jury cannot use an unseen photograph, and a complete evidence folder does not guarantee that the jury reasons correctly.

**Kitchen example:** if the sampler retrieves only the window-opening frame, “to cool the room” is a plausible guess caused by retrieval failure. If it retrieves the smoking pan and the open window but still gives that answer, the evidence is present and the failure is fusion. If giving the model the human-selected frames fixes the answer, the backbone already had enough reasoning ability for that example.

**The oracle-frame test:** for a small development set, label the minimum moments needed to answer. Run the model twice—once on its retrieved frames and once on the labeled frames. The gap between end-to-end and oracle-frame performance estimates the retrieval problem; errors that remain with oracle frames point toward fusion, prompting, or answer selection.

**What the literature adds:** [HERBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14870) explicitly separates missing-evidence and present-but-not-integrated failures. [FALCONEye](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19850) couples an open answer with a supporting temporal window. KFS-Bench provides scene-level targets for auditing selectors.

**Closest 2025 systems:** NII_UIT is the clearest evidence-engine baseline; HLTCOE is the clearest answer-selection baseline. Neither paper reports the oracle-frame diagnostic, so their score does not reveal which stage dominated errors.

**TRECVID test:** label required moments for 50–100 representative development questions. Report selector recall, oracle-frame answer quality, and normal end-to-end quality. Change the selector only when retrieval is weak; change reasoning or ranking only when oracle performance is weak.

## Idea 3 — Keep the whole timeline, then zoom into a few moments

Video understanding has two competing needs. **Global chronology** preserves which events happened and in what order. **Local detail** preserves small text, objects, facial expressions, hand actions, and screen content. Sending every moment at full resolution is usually wasteful; compressing everything can erase the exact detail the question needs.

**Everyday analogy:** a subway map shows the entire route but not the storefront beside one station. A street photograph shows that storefront but not where it sits in the journey. A useful evidence pack contains both: a map of the story and close-ups of selected stops.

**Kitchen example:** a small timeline panel may show smoke, the alarm reaction, and the open window in order. But the smoke may be only a few gray pixels, and the stove display or product label may be unreadable. After selecting the likely cause and outcome, the system can request native-resolution crops around the pan, alarm, hands, or window.

**What the literature adds:** [Video Panels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23724) packs multiple moments into compact panels for temporal coverage. [Qwen2.5-VL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13923) supports dynamic-resolution visual input, while [TimeChat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02051) emphasizes retaining timestamp identity rather than treating frames as an unordered gallery.

**Closest 2025 system:** NII_UIT explicitly combined time-spaced frames with spatial tiling. That is directionally close to global-plus-local evidence, although the paper does not isolate which part produced the gain.

**TRECVID test:** under one visual-token budget, compare separate global frames, compact panels, tiles for every selected frame, and global frames plus tiles only around question-relevant moments. Break out OCR, small-object, counting, and temporal questions; an aggregate score can hide the tradeoff.

## Idea 4 — A transcript and the soundtrack carry different evidence

**Automatic speech recognition (ASR)** converts spoken words into searchable text with timestamps. That is ideal for dialogue, narration, names, and verbal instructions. **Native audio** preserves signals that are not words: alarms, impacts, applause, music, animal sounds, silence, tone, speaker overlap, and the exact timing between sound and action.

**Everyday analogy:** a transcript is closed captions; native audio is the soundtrack. Reading “I am fine” does not reveal whether it was whispered, shouted, or sarcastic, and many systems omit a sound such as a beep entirely.

**Kitchen example:** Whisper may transcribe the person's speech but represent the alarm only as an uncertain tag—or omit it. Native audio can preserve that a sharp alarm began after the smoke and before the window opened. Conversely, native audio alone may make exact spoken words harder for a general video model to recover than a clean timestamped transcript.

**What the literature adds:** [Whisper](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/radford23a.html) provides a strong timestamped speech path. [Qwen2.5-Omni](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20215) is designed for time-aligned native audio and video. [Video-MME](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21075) demonstrates the value of matched visual-, subtitle-, and audio-condition evaluation rather than assuming one modality always helps.

**Closest 2025 systems:** NII_UIT and HLTCOE exposed transcript evidence; CERTH-ITI used a native audio-video model. These systems were not evaluated in a shared modality ablation, so the leaderboard cannot tell which audio representation was best.

**TRECVID test:** run the same frozen model and evidence sampler in four conditions: video only, video plus ASR, video plus native audio, and video plus both. Store transcript confidence and sound-event timestamps, then inspect dialogue, sound-event, causal, and temporal slices separately.

## Idea 5 — A causal answer needs an inspectable evidence chain

A model can produce a fluent explanation from general world knowledge without using the video. **Grounded causal reasoning** requires the answer to connect specific observed events and preserve where each claim came from. The goal is not a long hidden chain-of-thought; it is a short external receipt that another person or program can check.

**Kitchen example:** the evidence chain might be “pan begins smoking at 8 seconds → alarm sounds at 15 seconds → person opens the window at 27 seconds.” The answer “because the pan was smoking and triggered an alarm” is supported. “To cool the room” may be plausible in ordinary life, but the video evidence does not support it.

**Why order matters:** showing the smoke and window frames is not enough if their timestamps are lost or reversed. Cause should precede the response, and intervening evidence can distinguish a direct cause from a coincidence. A system should therefore keep frame IDs, timestamps, transcript spans, and audio-event times through every stage.

**What the literature adds:** [NExT-QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.08276) highlights the gap between describing actions and explaining temporal or causal relations. [CaST-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23216) makes cause-to-effect evidence chains explicit. [HERBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14870) makes several separated cues unavoidable.

**Closest 2025 systems:** every team could benefit from evidence traces, but the public papers mainly describe inputs and outputs rather than a scored causal chain. This is a frontier gap, not a claim that their answers were ungrounded.

**TRECVID test:** for a small causal slice, label two- or three-step evidence chains. Require each candidate answer to cite timestamps, then score answer correctness, evidence recall, order consistency, and performance when cited evidence is removed.

## Idea 6 — Brainstorming, judging, and confidence should be separate stages

**Generation** produces plausible candidates. **Election** chooses among them using evidence and agreement. **Calibration** checks whether the numerical confidence behaves like reliability rather than rewarding repetition, short answers, familiar phrasing, or a preferred MC option position.

**Everyday analogy:** brainstorming and judging are different meetings. The first benefits from diversity; the second needs a rubric. Counting identical wording is a weak vote because “because of smoke,” “the pan was smoking,” and “smoke triggered the alarm” may express the same underlying answer.

**Kitchen example:** suppose the model generates “to cool the room,” “because smoke filled the kitchen,” and “because the smoke alarm sounded.” Semantic clustering prevents paraphrases from occupying several AG ranks. Evidence-aware election prefers candidates that cite the smoking pan and alarm. For MC, shuffling A/B/C/D and mapping scores back reveals whether the model favors an answer position rather than the content.

**What the literature adds:** [VCSS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20472) and [Video Parallel Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08016) aggregate complementary visual views. [RADI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14430) studies open-answer ordering with incomplete labels. [RLER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04379) elects candidates using explicit evidence properties. [BOLD](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.162/) targets MC option-position bias.

**Closest 2025 systems:** CERTH-ITI used multi-view voting and score pooling; HLTCOE learned a listwise reranker; kslab used confidence and embedding similarity; WHU-NERCMS used a generated free-text anchor for MC matching. They are different approximations of an election layer.

**TRECVID test:** AG should generate more than ten candidates, cluster semantic duplicates, and compare confidence-only with evidence-aware ranking while reporting top-1, oracle-at-k, official top-10, and cost. MC should score options directly, permute their order, map scores back, and pool calibrated logits across evidence views.

The table below compresses the chapter into questions a team can answer from logs. It is deliberately stage-based: before replacing the backbone, ask whether the video decoded, whether the needed moments were selected, whether detail or sound was lost, whether the model could answer from oracle evidence, and whether a later election rule overrode a good candidate.

## The research threads translate into six controlled experiments

Each row below changes one major mechanism while holding the rest of the pipeline as stable as possible. The point is not to reproduce every paper. It is to borrow the diagnostic idea, test it under the TRECVID input and output contract, and retain it only if it improves the right slice at an acceptable cost.

## What to implement first

1. **First make evidence observable.** Cache global frames, timestamped ASR, selected-frame IDs, option scores, candidate answers, and a strict run manifest. A weak but inspectable baseline is more useful than a strong black box.
2. **Then improve retrieval at fixed cost.** Add the half-uniform plus half-question sampler and a small required-frame development set. Do not increase frames and change the selector in the same experiment.
3. **Add detail and audio only where diagnostics justify them.** Selective tiles target OCR and small objects; native audio targets sound-event and timing questions. Keep matched ablations so added modalities cannot receive credit merely for added compute.
4. **Add evidence traces before learned election.** Store candidate-to-evidence links and semantic clusters. Simple rules become strong baselines and create training targets for a later reranker.
5. **Train the complicated selector or ranker last.** Reinforcement-learning selectors and listwise rerankers are valuable only after a training-free alternative wins locally and the evaluation path is stable.

This order minimizes confounding: every added component has a logged input, a measurable job, and a rollback path.

## The 2025 teams sampled different pieces of this frontier

**CERTH-ITI** is closest to multi-view test-time scaling; **NII_UIT** is closest to question-conditioned evidence selection; **HLTCOE** is closest to answer-generation plus listwise ranking. **WHU-NERCMS** and **kslab** expose the risks of generate-then-embed MC ranking, while **tcna** is a useful proprietary ceiling with a reproducibility gap and **TJUMI** shows why fine-tuning cannot rescue an unreliable submission path.

The crosswalk below states what each lineage supports, what the published system still lacks, and one experiment that changes a single major variable for 2026. These are evidence-backed design hypotheses, not claims that a paper mechanism caused a team's leaderboard position.

## What does not transfer cleanly

- **Most VideoQA papers optimize one best MC answer.** TRECVID AG requires an ordered set of exactly ten open answers, so answer diversity and weak-tail control matter in a way most benchmarks do not measure.
- **Long-video gains are not automatically relevant to six-minute clips.** Retrieval and memory methods should first beat a repaired fixed-frame baseline at the same frame, runtime, and API-call budget.
- **Cross-paper score deltas are not comparable.** Datasets, option counts, video duration, modality access, model scale, and evaluation scripts differ; the table is a mechanism map, not a meta-analysis.
- **A fluent rationale is not evidence.** Store the timestamps, crops, transcript spans, and option scores that actually supported each answer; evaluate evidence recall separately whenever local labels permit.
- **Publication does not guarantee local transfer.** VCSS and Video Parallel Scaling are now peer-reviewed, but their sample-scaling mechanisms still need a controlled local ablation under TRECVID's frame, latency, and output constraints.

The deepest table is therefore ordered by **transfer fit** and practical learning value rather than by a synthetic paper ranking.

## Chapter 7 · Build one evidence engine and two thin task heads

The highest-leverage shared work is media reliability: download or locate each video, record availability and hashes, normalize codecs, extract timestamped automatic speech recognition (ASR) and optical character recognition (OCR) once, and cache global frames, shot-aware keyframes, and local tiles. A question router then chooses the evidence budget. The image below turns that plan into one phone-readable flow.

The competition-adjacent literature makes the routing rule more specific: guarantee broad coverage, add question-relevant moments, preserve high resolution only around likely evidence, retain both ASR and native audio, and spend extra views only when answer agreement is weak. For causal questions, keep the cause and outcome timestamps with each candidate rather than relying on an unsupported rationale.

For AG, generate 20–30 candidates efficiently, normalize without changing meaning, cluster near-duplicates, and rank exactly ten. For MC, preserve the four option strings byte-for-byte and aggregate direct option scores across evidence views. Both outputs pass a strict schema gate that fails loudly on missing IDs, invalid ranks, duplicate options, missing times, or fallback error text.

## Newcomer glossary

- **TREC / TRECVID:** the Text REtrieval Conference and its video-evaluation program.
- **NIST:** the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, which runs the evaluation.
- **VQA — Video Question Answering:** answer a question using evidence from a video.
- **AG — Answer Generation:** produce ranked free-text answers.
- **MC — Multiple Choice:** rank four supplied answer options.
- **Evalbase:** NIST's web portal for validating and submitting runs.
- **VLM / MLLM:** a vision-language or multimodal large language model that accepts visual and textual evidence; some models also accept audio.
- **Run:** one complete system-output file submitted for evaluation.
- **Ground truth:** the hidden reference answer used for scoring.
- **Fine-tuning:** updating model weights on task data; **inference-time scaling** instead repeats or enriches model calls without changing weights.
- **ASR / OCR:** automatic speech recognition turns audio into text; optical character recognition reads visible text in frames.
- **LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation:** a memory-efficient way to fine-tune a model.
- **TTA — test-time augmentation:** repeat inference under controlled input variations, such as reordering MC options, then combine the results.
- **MCOLL/KinoLorber:** the licensed movie collection named in organizer materials; access requires a signed agreement.
- **Reranker:** a second-stage model or rule that reorders generated answers or options.
- **Top-1:** the first-ranked item only. **MRR:** partial credit based on where the correct MC option appears. **NDCG:** a rank-quality score that rewards placing more relevant answers earlier.
